name: Jade Meridian

stars.name: Jade
stars.notes: Ancient orange dwarf with extremely low variability, has nurtured its biosphere for billions of years longer than Sol has existed

planets.name: Ember Root
planets.notes: Volcanic world with active silicate geysers. Mineral surveys indicate significant platinum group deposits.

planets.name: Verdance Minor
planets.notes: Dense jungle world orbiting close to the habitable zone's inner edge. Indigenous insectoid life forms have developed rudimentary tool use. Population 290 million in elevated canopy settlements.

planets.name: Pearlwater
planets.notes: Temperate ocean world with thousands of volcanic island chains. Rich marine biodiversity includes filter-feeding megafauna. Population 510 million across island and floating settlements.

planets.name: Ashveil
planets.notes: Thin CO2 atmosphere, heavily cratered. Serves as the system's primary mining extraction site for construction materials.

planets.name: Outerjade
planets.notes: Methane-rich ice world with spectacular azure surface coloring. Automated fuel extraction facilities harvest deuterium from subsurface deposits.

asteroid_belts.name: The Jade Belt
asteroid_belts.notes: Contains olivine-rich asteroids that give a distinctive green tint when illuminated. Small mining operations service the inner colonies.

stations.name: Meridian Gate
stations.notes: System's primary trade hub, specializing in marine biological exports and xenobiological samples under strict Conservancy licensing.

stations.name: Canopy Watch
stations.notes: Dedicated xenoanthropology station monitoring the indigenous tool-using insectoid species. Contact protocols are strictly enforced.

stations.name: Ashveil Depot
stations.notes: Mining operations hub providing raw materials for station construction and orbital infrastructure throughout the system.

faction_control.notes: Military-scientific governance with primary mandate to protect indigenous intelligent life on Verdance Minor. Non-interference protocols modeled on Earth historical precedents.

history: Survey teams in 2253 identified tool-using behavior in Verdance Minor's insectoid species, triggering immediate classification as a Protected Contact System under interstellar law.
Colonization was permitted only on Pearlwater and in elevated canopy zones of Verdance Minor where indigenous populations are absent, with strict no-contact buffer zones enforced since 2261.
The discovery of the insectoids' rudimentary agriculture in 2299 elevated the system's scientific importance, drawing xenoanthropologists from across known space.
description: Jade Meridian takes its name from the green-tinged light of its ancient orange star, filtered through the olivine-rich asteroid belt that circles the inner system like an emerald ring. Five worlds orbit this venerable sun, two of them alive—one with complex marine ecosystems, the other harboring what may be humanity's most significant xenobiological discovery: an insectoid species on the cusp of civilization. The system is compact by galactic standards, its habitable zone nestled close to the cool star, but what it lacks in scale it compensates for in biological richness.

Verdance Minor is the system's crown jewel and its greatest responsibility. The insectoid species—formally designated Viridoptera meridiani—builds shelters from woven plant fibers, cultivates fungal gardens, and communicates through complex pheromone patterns. Human settlements perch in the upper canopy, kilometers above the forest floor where the Viridoptera live, connected by aerial tramways that cast no shadow on the world below. Pearlwater offers a different kind of wonder: volcanic island chains where terrestrial and marine ecosystems interweave, and filter-feeding leviathans breach the surface in displays that draw visitors from dozens of systems.

The tension in Jade Meridian is one of restraint. Every scientist wants closer access to the Viridoptera; every corporation eyes the biological wealth locked in two living worlds; every settler chafes at the Protectorate's restrictions. Yet the system holds firm to its founding principle: these worlds were alive long before humanity arrived, and they must remain so long after. The debate over whether to attempt communication with the Viridoptera—or to simply observe for another century—defines the system's politics and may ultimately define its place in history.
